match.reason: None of the bank points teaches filling a matrix from an element rule such as 2i + j; the closest, Matrix operations, covers order, addition and multiplication but not building a matrix from a rule.

draft.title: Building a matrix from a rule
card: The element in row i and column j is written aᵢⱼ. The first number, i, is the row. The second number, j, is the column.
A rule gives aᵢⱼ in terms of i and j. To build the matrix, put each row number and column number into the rule, one position at a time.
The order tells you how many rows and columns to fill. A 2 × 3 matrix has i = 1, 2 and j = 1, 2, 3.
Example: for a 2 × 2 matrix with aᵢⱼ = 2i + j, a₁₁ = 2(1) + 1 = 3, a₁₂ = 2(1) + 2 = 4, a₂₁ = 2(2) + 1 = 5 and a₂₂ = 2(2) + 2 = 6. The matrix has rows [3 4] and [5 6].
draft.remember: Put the row number in for i and the column number in for j, then fill the matrix position by position.

a.q: A 2 × 3 matrix has the rule aᵢⱼ = i + 3j. What is the element a₂₁?
a.why: a₂₁ has i = 2 and j = 1, so a₂₁ = 2 + 3(1) = 5. The answer 7 comes from swapping the numbers, which gives i = 1 and j = 2: 1 + 3(2) = 7.
a.clue: The first number in 21 is the row, and the second is the column.

b.q: A 2 × 2 matrix B has the rule bᵢⱼ = 3i − j. What is the sum of all four elements of B?
b.why: b₁₁ = 2, b₁₂ = 1, b₂₁ = 5 and b₂₂ = 4. The sum is 2 + 1 + 5 + 4 = 12. Check: 3 × (1 + 1 + 2 + 2) − (1 + 2 + 1 + 2) = 18 − 6 = 12. The option 14 comes from mixing up i and j.
b.clue: Find each element one at a time, then add them.

problems.detail: The why says 14 comes from mixing up i and j, but this is false. Using 3j − i gives 2, 5, 1 and 4, which also sum to 12, so no option matches that error and the explanation would mislead students.

Because the sum of all elements is the same whether or not i and j are swapped, this question cannot catch the row–column mix-up the point is meant to teach. Asking for a single off-diagonal element, or for the matrix itself, would test the idea.

check.summary: Both answers are correct (a = 5, b = 12), but the why for (b) wrongly says 14 comes from swapping i and j; swapping still gives 12. Question (b) also cannot detect that mix-up because the sum does not change when i and j are swapped.

b.q: A 2 × 3 matrix B has the rule bᵢⱼ = 3i − j. What is row 2 of B?
b.why: In row 2, i = 2 and j runs from 1 to 3: b₂₁ = 6 − 1 = 5, b₂₂ = 6 − 2 = 4 and b₂₃ = 6 − 3 = 3. The option [1 4 7] comes from mixing up i and j and using 3j − i instead. The option [2 1 0] is row 1, not row 2.
b.clue: Along a row, which of i and j stays the same?
